newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition calls on forces to take stand.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition calls on forces to take stand.

text.p: Serbia's opposition, planning a huge Orthodox New Year's Eve rally, urged the army and police on Monday to quickly declare their position on alleged demands by powerful leftists that eight-week-old protests be crushed.

"Top officials of the Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) and the Yugoslav United Left (JUL) are demanding that the police use force to crush demonstrations in Serbia," the Zajedno (Together) coalition said in a statement.
Zajedno alleged that SPS and JUL were "obviously seeking to provoke large conflicts and impose an official state of emergency in Serbia.

"The coalition therefore demands that the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and the Serbian Interior Ministry protect the citizens and state interests of Serbia, which are being openly attacked and jeopardised by the SPS and JUL."
Zajedno did not reveal the source of its information on an alleged state plan to crack down on the pro-democracy rallies.
But respected independent media have reported that a hard-line faction, concentrated in JUL, was pushing for drastic police action to get protesters off the streets.

However, support for violent repression was believed to be weak in the army and not as strong in the security police as in similar situations earlier in the decade-old rule of autocratic President Slobodan Milosevic.

At a recent meeting with Belgrade students, who have sided with Zajedno in their peaceful daily protests, Yugoslav army chief General Momcilo Perisic said the military would stay neutral, tacitly backing the protesters.

Authoritative sources say most army officers would not back Milosevic after he humiliated them with widespread purges of their ranks after the unsuccessful 1991 war over Croatia's secession from Yugoslavia.
Milosevic has marginalised the once fourth-largest army in Europe in favour of the better paid, 100,000-strong and better equipped security police force.
Police have so far exercised notable restraint except for random beatings meted out one night by plainclothes thugs.
Senior security chiefs distanced themselves from that action, betraying potential rifts in police ranks as well.
Zajedno is demonstrating to press its claim to have won 14 of Serbia's 18 largest cities including the capital Belgrade in municipal elections on November 17 later annulled by the SPS.
The ruling party's move triggered a wave of daily street protests -- the most serious challenge to leftist rule in Serbia stretching back to 1945.
Sceptical of Milosevic's intentions, Zajedno urged hundreds of thousands of people to turn out on Monday for an Orthodox New Year's Eve demonstration in the biggest show of strength yet.
The opposition previously drew hundreds of thousands of people to central Belgrade for demonstrations on the eve of Orthodox Christmas, celebrated on January 7.

Analysts said Milosevic was hesitating before steps to end Serbia's worst political crisis in a decade for several reasons, including divisions within ruling parties and a lack of resolve by the Contact Group of Western powers and Russia.
"It is a holy mess. It is the mother of all confusions. Decisions are being made and changed on a daily basis and no one really knows what to do," a senior political source told Reuters on Monday.
"Many are going to come out of this fiercely burned," he said, referring to infighting between moderates and authoritarian hardliners in the SPS and JUL.

"They are fighting for their very lives especially after a point where Milosevic was close to endorsing the opposition victory," the source said, adding Milosevic would have conceded only to student and not Zajedno demands to save face.
"The hardliners persuaded him against acting "hastily' when the Contact Group said on Saturday it will not impose sanctions (for the time being) on Belgrade," the official said.
A few prominent SPS and other establishment figures have openly called for restoring Zajedno's victories.

They include Nebojsa Covic, the moderate mayor of Belgrade; Ratko Markovic and Nedeljko Sipovac, two deputy prime ministers who on Saturday promised to fulfil student demands for "genuine and final" election results to be honoured; and Dusan Mitevic, former state television chief and a close Milosevic friend.
